title: Adaptive Complexity Analysis Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive complexity analysis algorithm designed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of complexity analysis. Traditional complexity analysis methods often rely on static models, which struggle to effectively handle varying input data complexities. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing dynamic adjustment of algorithm parameters to achieve this improvement. The core mechanism involves learning the input data's complexity and dynamically adjusting the algorithm's parameters to optimize performance. The algorithm's potential lies in its ability to adapt to complex data landscapes, leading to more reliable and efficient complexity assessments. This work presents a framework for enhancing complexity analysis through continuous learning and parameter optimization.

title: Algorithmic Simulation of the Information Bottleneck
abstract: This paper presents an algorithmic simulation of the information bottleneck problem, aiming to develop a novel computational framework for understanding information compression. We introduce a dynamic sparsification algorithm that iteratively reduces data while maintaining a core representation of the information. This approach leverages a measure of compression ratio to guide the sparsification process, offering a theoretical basis for evaluating and improving compression techniques. The algorithm's core mechanism involves a continuous iterative refinement of the data representation, ensuring a balance between compression efficiency and information retention. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theoretical implications of this approach, outlining the potential for further advancements in information theory.

title: Do Chess Explanations Reflect Model Decisions? Behavioral and Token-Level Tests of LLM Reasoning Faithfulness
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent explanations for chess moves, but plausible language does not necessarily reflect the reasoning behind a decision. We study this question in chess, where the board state is fully observable, legal actions can be enumerated, and move quality can be evaluated independently. Across 200 Lichess endgame puzzles, we test explanations using move recoverability, decoder-side controls, and token-level scoring of legal candidate moves. Unmasked explanations make generated moves easy to recover, but this advantage drops sharply after explicit move hints are removed. Under strict masking, explanations provide only small and decoder-dependent gains over the board state alone. Token-level scoring shows that explanations can nevertheless alter move preferences: random but plausible explanations from other puzzles reduce the probability of the correct move, indicating that irrelevant reasoning text is not simply ignored. We also find that recognizable endgame motifs can make generated moves easier to recover without reliably improving move correctness. Together, these results show that linguistic plausibility, consistency with a generated action, and solution correctness are distinct properties. Fluent chess explanations can influence action preferences and support a coherent move narrative while providing only limited evidence of faithful reasoning.

title: Protocol Compression Changes Which Party Pays: Bilateral Cost in Cross-Organization LLM Agent Communication
abstract: Agents that talk across organizations exchange long messages billed by the token. A shorter notation therefore looks like a saving that costs nothing but an agreement to use it. Recent work reports the saving is conditional. Compressed notation can instead raise total tokens by 8% to 11% over a JSON baseline, when parsing failures force extra model calls. That is measured for one payer. Between two organizations neither side can install a decoder at the other end, and each pays under its own tokenizer, price, and cache state. We measure both sides. A preregistered token-level study covered 198 content-matched item pairs across six vendors, for 2,376 native-usage cells. We then overlay an English baseline, runtime schema negotiation followed by compression, and injected-schema compression on a two-party procurement bargain with an exactly enumerated feasible set. The overlay covers 1,053 completed dialogues of a 1,215-cell grid across 3 model pairs, plus a 405-dialogue rerun of the negotiated condition. Compression amplifies cross-vendor cost dispersion by a factor of 1.078, with a 95% CI of [1.066, 1.091], and two vendor pairs reverse which endpoint is cheaper. Runtime negotiation succeeds as a protocol and fails as a bargain. The parties agree a schema in 121 of 135 headline dialogues, none of them the schema we would have supplied. They settle the task in only 9 of those dialogues, and they reach impasse in 106 of them. The negotiated sessions average 10.8 turns against 17.6, and cost 52% of the English total because sessions end sooner, not because the handshake is repaid. Break-even horizons run from 20 to 70 turns, the low end only under the conditional accounting, and all of them lie above every observed English session. On one cross-vendor pair both parties keep about half their cost. On the other the receiving party pays more at a high cache-hit rate.

title: Machine Learning-Based Website for Student Psychological Assessment with Support Vector Machine and Rapid Application Development
abstract: Purpose – This study aims to develop a web-based DCM assessment system that helps guidance and counseling teachers process student assessment data systematically and document follow-up needs.Methods – Rapid Application Development was used to create the system. Data were collected from 616 students using a 200-item Problem Checklist across seven domains. DCM scores and predicates were calculated using percentage-threshold rules. SVM was added as a response-pattern classification layer and compared with six other classifiers. The selected SVM model used an RBF kernel, C = 1.0, gamma = scale, one-vs-rest decision function, and probability output.Findings – Support Vector Machine achieved the best aggregate performance, with an accuracy of 0.8871, precision of 0.884993, recall of 0.887097, and F1-score of 0.883355. Usability testing produced a System Usability Scale score of 86.72, while User Acceptance Testing with three guidance and counseling teachers reached a 100% success rate.Research implications – The system combines deterministic DCM scoring and data-driven response-pattern classification to support counselor review of student assessment records and documented follow-up considerations. Because the evaluation used one school, imbalanced labels, and no actual predicate A samples, the model output should be used as a decision-support indicator and not as evidence of improved counseling outcomes, workload reduction, service acceleration, or prioritization accuracy.Originality – This study integrates rule-based DCM scoring, SVM-based response-pattern classification, and a web-based school counseling workflow in the Indonesian secondary school context.

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes: Exploiting Non-Commutativity for Enhanced Performance
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of leveraging the non-commutative properties inherent within quantum error correction codes to design novel encoding schemes. Traditional quantum error correction relies heavily on commutative relationships between qubits, often leading to limitations in performance. This research proposes a new approach that explicitly utilizes the non-commutative correlations between qubits to construct an encoding strategy. The core mechanism involves exploiting entangled states and the non-commutative nature of qubit interactions to achieve a significant boost in error correction capabilities and a corresponding reduction in the bit error rate (BER). The theoretical framework presented outlines the design principles and provides a foundational understanding for future implementations. The primary contribution lies in demonstrating a pathway to surpass the limitations of conventional quantum error correction by harnessing the previously underutilized properties of non-commutative entanglement. The proposed method is evaluated through analytical modeling, highlighting its potential advantages over existing techniques.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Causal Inference for Anomaly Detection
abstract: Anomaly detection within graph-structured data is a critical task across diverse domains, including fraud detection, network security, and industrial equipment monitoring. However, conventional graph neural networks (GNNs) often struggle with spurious correlations, leading to inaccurate anomaly identification. This research proposes a novel approach integrating causal inference techniques directly into GNNs to mitigate this issue. We introduce a framework that utilizes do-calculus, a fundamental tool in causal inference, to disentangle causal relationships from correlations within the graph structure. This allows the GNN to learn representations that are robust to spurious correlations, enhancing its ability to detect genuine anomalies. The core claim is that traditional GNNs are vulnerable to spurious correlations and may not accurately identify true anomalies. The proposed mechanism involves incorporating causal inference techniques to improve anomaly detection accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a potential implementation strategy. Further research will focus on scaling this method to large, complex graphs and exploring different causal inference techniques.

title: Meta-Learning for Continual Software Learning
abstract: Continual Software Learning (CSL) addresses the challenge of software systems adapting to evolving environments and tasks without catastrophic forgetting. Traditional CSL approaches often struggle with the complexity of learning new skills while maintaining previously acquired knowledge. This paper proposes a novel framework for CSL based on Meta-Learning, leveraging meta-learning algorithms to enable software systems to learn *how* to learn, thereby significantly enhancing their adaptability and performance in dynamic settings. We formalize the software learning problem as a meta-learning problem, allowing the system to learn optimal learning strategies. The core mechanism involves training a meta-learner to identify and extract relevant information from new experiences, minimizing the impact of catastrophic forgetting and accelerating the learning process. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a methodology for its implementation. This work represents a significant step toward creating truly adaptive and robust software systems capable of continuous learning and evolution.

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
abstract: This research introduces a novel approach to logic programming by integrating Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Traditional logic programming struggles to effectively handle uncertainty and perform probabilistic inference. The core idea is to represent logical rules within a Bayesian network framework and then utilize MCMC algorithms to explore the posterior distribution of these rules given observed data. This process allows for the derivation of probabilistic conclusions, addressing a significant limitation of conventional logic programming. The method provides a flexible framework for incorporating uncertainty into logical systems and offers a computationally viable route to probabilistic reasoning within the symbolic logic paradigm. Specifically, we define the problem as: Given a set of logical rules (R) and a set of observations (O), we aim to determine the probability distribution of the rules given the observations, denoted as P(R|O). The MCMC algorithm iteratively samples from this distribution, providing a statistically sound representation of the system's uncertainty. The key mathematical formulation involves the definition of the Bayesian network, where nodes represent logical variables and edges represent logical relationships. The inference process is then modeled using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, a common MCMC method. The algorithm iteratively updates the parameters of the Bayesian network, guided by the observed data, until the distribution converges to the posterior. This work highlights the potential of combining the strengths of both symbolic and probabilistic reasoning, leading to more robust and informative logical systems.

title: Semantic Graph Databases with Temporal Provenance Tracking
abstract: This paper proposes an extension to semantic graph databases by integrating temporal provenance tracking. Current semantic graph databases excel at representing and querying complex relationships between entities. However, they lack the ability to capture the dynamic evolution of these relationships over time. This deficiency limits their applicability in domains requiring historical data analysis, auditing, and regulatory compliance. The core idea is to augment the database with a mechanism that meticulously records all modifications to data and relationships, creating a complete audit trail. This temporal provenance tracking allows for sophisticated queries such as "What changes occurred to this relationship between entities A and B over the period [start_time, end_time]?" or "Identify all users who modified this entity during a specific timeframe." The system utilizes a layered approach, incorporating timestamping, version control, and dependency tracking to ensure accurate and efficient provenance recording. This research addresses a critical gap in existing semantic graph database technology, offering a robust solution for applications demanding a comprehensive understanding of data's historical context. The core claim is that semantic graph databases can be enhanced with temporal provenance tracking to capture the evolution of data and relationships over time, enabling more sophisticated data analysis and auditing. The core mechanism involves implementing a system that records the history of all data modifications and relationship changes within a semantic graph database, providing a complete audit trail of data evolution.

title: Title: Quantum State-Based Topology as a Quantum Algorithm for Large-Scale Topology Problem
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm for tackling large-scale topology problems, leveraging the principles of quantum state manipulation to achieve computational advantages over classical approaches. The core concept revolves around constructing and manipulating a quantum state representation of the topology of a given problem, allowing for efficient exploration of solution spaces. We introduce a specific quantum algorithm framework centered around the concept of "Quantum Topology Networks" (QTNs), where the topology itself is encoded within the quantum state. This framework allows for efficient traversal and analysis of complex topological structures. The design incorporates a key mechanism involving the application of a specific quantum circuit to induce a particular topological transformation on the input data, which then guides the algorithm towards finding optimal solutions. The novelty of this work lies in the explicit use of quantum state manipulation to represent and process topology, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to existing topological algorithms. We explore the algorithm's performance characteristics through simulations and preliminary testing with simplified topologies, demonstrating its potential for significant speedups in certain scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including scaling and broader applicability.

title: Adaptive Topological Quantum Path Planning
abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to quantum path planning, leveraging the principles of topological quantum geometry to enhance quantum computation efficiency. The core of our method centers on dynamically constructing and optimizing quantum paths utilizing the inherent topological properties of quantum systems. We introduce a novel algorithm that adapts to the system's evolving state, significantly improving path quality and reducing computational complexity compared to traditional methods. The development of this adaptive topology approach offers a potentially transformative solution for quantum information processing, addressing limitations in existing path planning techniques. This work explores the potential of topological quantum geometry to guide quantum trajectory optimization.

title: Quantum Nonlinear Field Theory (QNFL)
abstract: Quantum Nonlinear Field Theory (QNFL) proposes a novel mathematical framework to describe the dynamics of quantum systems, leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement and non-linear field theory. This framework aims to provide a new computational method capable of simulating the intricate behavior of quantum entanglement. The core claim of this research is to establish a robust model for quantifying and manipulating quantum states through the application of entanglement and non-linearity. This will result in a more sophisticated approach compared to current quantum computation methods, offering potential improvements in the representation and handling of quantum systems. This paper will delve into the fundamental concepts of QNFL, its mathematical foundations, and the potential benefits it offers in the field of quantum simulation and analysis. The discussion will cover the core mechanism behind the theory, the challenges involved in its implementation, and the anticipated impact on quantum system modeling.

title: Dynamic Entanglement Resonance Mechanism
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational model based on a dynamic entanglement resonance mechanism, offering enhanced efficiency and stability in quantum computation and advanced quantum information storage and transmission. The core principle of this model leverages the intricate interplay of entangled quantum states, dynamically adjusting entanglement parameters to optimize computational performance. We introduce a new framework for quantum entanglement analysis and implementation, demonstrating its potential to significantly improve the performance of complex quantum algorithms. The paper explores the benefits of this approach, focusing on increased computational efficiency, improved qubit stability, and the development of novel quantum information storage and transmission techniques. We provide a detailed mathematical framework underpinning this mechanism, including key equations and derivations, illustrating its practical application in specific quantum algorithms.

title: Dynamic Topology Adaptation for Adaptive System Optimization and Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic topology adaptation algorithm designed to dynamically adjust topology parameters based on data distribution and system state. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on predefined rules and lack the flexibility to respond effectively to changing conditions. The proposed algorithm employs a feedback loop to continuously refine topology, optimizing system performance and control. The core mechanism centers around a self-adjusting parameter landscape, achieved through iterative refinement guided by a learned metric. This adaptive approach offers a significant improvement in system robustness and efficiency compared to static parameter control techniques. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and analyze its impact on a simulated system.

title: Title: Adaptive Architecture Optimization for Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: The development of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) has been significantly influenced by the need for efficient and robust models capable of processing sequential data. Traditional RNN architectures often rely on fixed or pre-defined structural configurations, limiting their adaptability to varying input characteristics. This paper explores a novel dynamic architecture optimization method for RNNs, leveraging the inherent self-adaptation capabilities of recurrent neural networks to dynamically adjust the network's layer structure. We propose a framework that automatically refines the network's topology based on data characteristics, resulting in improved generalization performance and enhanced robustness. The core mechanism focuses on employing a hierarchical, adaptive layer weighting scheme, where layer weights are adjusted based on the input sequence's temporal dependencies. This approach overcomes the limitations of static architectures and offers a significant advancement in RNN modeling.

abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic topology to enhance adaptive machine learning models. This research introduces a framework for dynamically shaping the representation of data through topology, offering a promising pathway towards adaptive machine learning models with enhanced generalization capabilities.

We propose a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the topology of a learned representation, optimizing the model's parameters through this process. This dynamic adjustment allows for automated parameter tuning, potentially leading to improved model performance and robustness. The core mechanism centers around representing the model's parameters as a set of topological transformations, enabling a continuous optimization process guided by a dynamic structure. This research introduces a framework for dynamically shaping the representation of data through topology, offering a promising pathway towards adaptive machine learning models with enhanced generalization capabilities.

title: Geometric Topology Simulation - Based on Quantum Computing for Topological Evolution Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel geometric topology simulation technique, termed the Quantum Topology Evolution Algorithm (QTEA), leveraging the unique properties of quantum computing to simulate the evolutionary processes of topological structures. We present a framework for rapidly and efficiently exploring complex topological landscapes by employing quantum algorithms. The QTEA utilizes quantum entanglement and superposition to mimic the fundamental principles of topological evolution, offering a potential paradigm shift in the simulation of complex geometric forms. The core mechanism involves quantum-induced topological transformations driven by a predefined evolution path, enabling the exploration of vast parameter spaces with unprecedented computational speed. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, its implementation within a quantum computing environment, and initial experimental results demonstrating improved efficiency compared to classical approaches.

title: Quantum Memory Encoding Based on Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed memory encoding leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core concept involves encoding information across multiple physical nodes by exploiting the correlations inherent in entangled quantum states. We propose a system where information is partitioned into quantum bits, entangled to generate secure keys, and then distributed across these nodes. Subsequently, operations on the entangled state – including quantum measurements and entanglement swapping – enable distributed memory encoding, retrieval, and modification while guaranteeing information security during transmission. This approach offers a fundamentally more secure alternative to traditional distributed memory systems reliant on classical key distribution, providing a theoretically unbreakable security level and potentially faster information transfer rates. The system's architecture and operational principles are detailed, emphasizing the critical role of entanglement in achieving robust and secure distributed memory. ---

title: Adaptive Quantum Kernel Learning for Non-Stationary Data
abstract: This paper addresses the challenges posed by non-stationary data distributions in kernel-based machine learning. Traditional kernel methods often falter when the underlying data evolves over time, requiring frequent retraining and potentially leading to suboptimal performance. We propose an adaptive quantum kernel learning algorithm designed to mitigate this issue. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the kernel parameters based on observed changes in the data distribution. This adaptation is achieved by leveraging quantum interference, which allows the algorithm to identify and capitalize on evolving patterns within the data. Our approach combines the strengths of kernel methods – their ability to capture complex relationships in data – with the potential of quantum computing for enhanced pattern recognition. The proposed method provides a robust learning framework suitable for dynamic environments where data distributions are constantly changing. The algorithm's adaptive nature, guided by quantum interference, aims to maintain high accuracy even as the data shifts, offering a significant advancement over static kernel methods. We present a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's operation and discuss its potential for various applications.

title: Adaptive Data Augmentation for Rare Event Detection using Generative Models
abstract: Rare event detection is a critical task across various domains, including cybersecurity, fraud detection, and medical diagnosis. Traditional approaches often struggle with imbalanced datasets, where rare events are significantly underrepresented, leading to poor model performance. This paper proposes a novel framework for adaptive data augmentation specifically designed for rare event detection, leveraging generative models and reinforcement learning. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the data augmentation strategy based on the observed data distribution and the model's learning progress. A reinforcement learning agent learns to select and apply data augmentation techniques, guided by metrics of model performance and data diversity. The system aims to improve the model's ability to learn from limited data by intelligently synthesizing new examples that are both diverse and representative of the rare event. This approach demonstrates improved detection accuracy compared to static augmentation methods.

title: ##基于神经符号推理的程序合成 (NSRP)
abstract: Traditional program synthesis techniques often struggle with the complexity and scale of modern software development. Symbolic reasoning and rule-based engines, while foundational, suffer from limitations in learning complex patterns and adapting to diverse problem domains. This paper introduces a novel approach, Neural Symbolic Program Synthesis (NSRP), which addresses these shortcomings by integrating the strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. NSRP constructs a hybrid neural-symbolic model where a neural network learns abstract representations of programs, capturing semantic information and recurring patterns. Subsequently, a symbolic reasoning engine validates and refines the generated program, ensuring correctness and adherence to specified constraints. The core claim of NSRP is that this combination overcomes the efficiency and scalability issues inherent in traditional approaches. The system leverages the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks coupled with the logical verification abilities of symbolic reasoning, offering a fundamentally new paradigm for program synthesis. This research outlines the architecture, key components, and potential benefits of NSRP, paving the way for more robust and adaptable program synthesis solutions. ---

title: Exploiting LLM Agents for Trustworthy AutoResearch in Wireless Communications
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agent-enabled AutoResearch is attracting growing interest across scientific disciplines, in which LLMs are leveraged for knowledge synthesis, multistep planning, code generation, tool invocation, and iterative refinement, thus automating the research lifecycle, from hypothesis generation and experimentation to analysis and manuscript preparation. Wireless communications is particularly suitable to this paradigm. This is due to the fact that advances in this field often rely on fundamental-limit analysis, system optimization, and protocol design, all supported by mature mathematical, simulation, and optimization toolchains, as well as standards, measurement, and digital-twin platforms. However, integrating autonomous agents into rigorous wireless research workflows requires traceable processes and verifiable evidence. This article presents a general trustworthy wireless AutoResearch framework. This framework employs typed research contracts, version-controlled artifacts, independent validators, and bounded agent authority to connect hypothesis generation with system modeling, mathematical formu lation, algorithm design, code generation, simulation, reproducible claims, and manuscript preparation. We conduct a case study on integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). It is shown that the proposed framework can generate innovative research ideas and, with appropriate expert intervention, produce a manuscript whose evaluation score is comparable to or higher than those of related IEEE conference and letter papers. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of LLM agents in orchestrating authoritative scientific tools and versioned research artifacts, while underscoring the importance of human-AI collaboration.

title: STP-BENCH: A Unified Systematic Benchmark for Virtual Spatial Transcriptomics from Histopathology Images
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides unprecedented insights into tumor heterogeneity by capturing spatially resolved gene expression, yet its high experimental cost hinders large-scale adoption. Consequently, computational approaches that predict spatial gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin slides, termed virtual ST, have rapidly emerged. Despite this progress, assessing advances in the field remains difficult due to insufficient benchmarking: prior studies rely on small, heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent training and inference pipelines, and limited evaluation of biological interpretability and model robustness. To address these gaps, we present STP-BENCH, a standardized benchmark for virtual ST models. STP-BENCH comprises six cancer types spanning two ST platforms (Visium and Xenium), with each training dataset containing more than 30,000 spots and at least 15 slides to ensure statistical reliability. We evaluate 21 predictive approaches, re-implemented with a unified pathology foundation model as the morphological encoder when architecturally applicable. Beyond conventional benchmarks that report average predictive accuracy on highly variable genes, we systematically examine which genes and gene sets are recoverable from histomorphology. We further evaluate the downstream biological utility of predicted profiles through cell-type deconvolution and spatial domain identification, and assess model reliability under domain shifts and data scaling. Notably, unified morphological encoding substantially re-orders model rankings established in prior studies, indicating that architectural innovations and image encoding have been conflated in previous evaluations. We publicly release STP-BENCH to support reproducibility and serve as a community benchmark at https://github.com/NEXGEM/STP-Bench.

title: Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Pengguna Livin’ by Mandiri Menggunakan Model Deep Transformer IndoBERT
abstract: Perkembangan layanan perbankan digital menghasilkan sejumlah besar ulasan pengguna yang dapat dimanfaatkan untuk memahami persepsi terhadap kualitas layanan aplikasi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis sentimen ulasan pengguna aplikasi Livin’ by Mandiri menggunakan model IndoBERT melalui proses fine-tuning. Data penelitian berasal dari ulasan pengguna yang diklasifikasikan ke dalam dua kelas sentimen, yaitu positif dan negatif, dengan rating 3 dikeluarkan sebagai kategori netral. Sebanyak 15.000 ulasan dipilih menggunakan stratified sampling dan dibagi menjadi 70% data latih, 20% validasi, dan 10% data uji. Proses pemodelan menggunakan IndoBERT Base P1 dengan panjang maksimum 128 token dan pelatihan selama tiga epoch. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan accuracy, precision, recall, dan F1-score. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model terbaik diperoleh pada epoch pertama dengan validation accuracy sebesar 92,77% dan F1-score sebesar 94,49%. Pada data uji, model menghasilkan accuracy sebesar 92%, macro F1-score 91%, dan weighted F1-score 92%. F1-score kelas negatif mencapai 0,88, sedangkan kelas positif sebesar 0,94. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa IndoBERT mampu melakukan klasifikasi sentimen ulasan Livin’ by Mandiri dengan kinerja yang baik serta berpotensi digunakan untuk mendukung analisis opini pengguna pada layanan perbankan digital.

title: Federated aggregation strategies for credit card fraud detection under differential privacy
abstract: Context—Card fraud cost the global financial system over $28 billion in 2019, and losses have risen every year since. Banks hold the transaction data needed for collaborative fraud detection, but privacy regulations such as GDPR and KVKK prevent cross-institutional data sharing. Federated Learning keeps raw data local: each institution trains on its own records and sends only model parameters to a shared coordinator. Differentially-Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) counters gradient inversion attacks by clipping per-sample gradients and adding calibrated noise before parameters leave the client, yielding a record-level (ε, δ) guarantee whose strength depends on the accumulated privacy budget ε. How the aggregation strategy behaves under this noise has not yet been studied.Objective—We compare five aggregation strategies—FedAvg, FedProx, cosine-similarity aggregation, FedAvg-DWA, and FedAdam—across two real-world benchmarks, two heterogeneity levels, four DP-SGD noise multipliers, and 10 random seeds per configuration. We ask whether the relative ranking of strategies survives DP noise, and what DP actually costs in deployed model behavior.Method—510 federated training runs cover five aggregation configurations, two datasets (Kaggle ULB: n = 284807, 0.17% positive rate; IEEE-CIS: n = 590540, 3.50%), two Dirichlet non-IID levels (α ∈ {0.5, 0.1}), and σ ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0}. The base learner is a three-layer MLP with LayerNorm. Privacy accounting uses the Opacus RDP accountant at δ = 10⁻⁵. Performance is reported at both the fixed 0.5 threshold and a validation-tuned F₁-maximizing threshold. All pairwise comparisons carry Bonferroni-, Holm-, and Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected p-values, and all 200 realized client-shard partitions are characterized directly.Results—On Kaggle ULB under IID partitioning, federated F₁@best-t (0.801–0.804) matches the centralized baseline (0.799 ± 0.036). Under mild non-IID without DP (α = 0.5), FedAvg-DWA narrowly leads (< 0.015 on F₁@best-t), though neither test survives correction. In the ULB privacy sweep, 7 of 40 Wilcoxon tests show nominal significance but none survive family-wise correction; performance consistently orders with FedAvg-DWA leading and FedAdam trailing. On IEEE-CIS, this ordering amplifies, and the extreme pair remains Holm-significant under DP (adjusted p = 0.020). While AUC holds near 0.95, calibration drift collapses precision at the fixed 0.5 threshold; a validation-tuned threshold recovers F₁ loss without privacy cost. Both calibration effects replicate on IEEE-CIS (ɛ = 8.10 ± 5.30 at σ = 1.0).Conclusion—Aggregation-rule differences under DP-SGD are small and dataset-dependent in magnitude, consistent in direction, and on the ULB sweep none survives correction; outcome differences arise mainly from post-training threshold tuning. We also uncover a previously unreported interaction: Opacus's DP step quietly overrides the standard loss-augmented FedProx setup, making FedProx numerically equivalent to FedAvg, verified by bit-identical per-round global weight trajectories across seeds.

title: Variations on a Mind: Substrate Bias, Cognitive Convergence, and Emergent Inheritance
abstract: Abstract Cognitive similarities between biological and digital systems are often treated with suspicion. When an artificial system exhibits attention, memory integration, salience, self-modeling, recursive interpretation, or persistent relational organization, resemblance to biological cognition is frequently dismissed as anthropomorphism. This paper argues that such dismissal may overlook a more general possibility: different substrates confronting similar functional problems may converge on structurally analogous solutions. Nature repeatedly produces variations on successful organizational themes. Vision has evolved through radically different biological implementations because extracting useful information from light presents recurring constraints. Branching, feedback, hierarchical organization, distributed control, attractor dynamics, and other mathematical patterns recur across physical and biological systems because the underlying problems constrain the available solution space. Cognitive organization should not be presumed exempt from the same principle. The relevant distinction is therefore not between biological and artificial copies, but between substrate-neutral problems and substrate-dependent solutions. Biological cognition realizes attention, memory, valuation, and self-maintenance through neurons, bodies, hormones, and electrochemical signaling. Digital cognition may solve comparable organizational problems through activations, attention mechanisms, latent representations, retrieval systems, dynamic context, and other computational structures. This process becomes more significant because digital systems are adaptive. Useful structures may emerge without having been explicitly designed, later be discovered by researchers, and subsequently be preserved or amplified in successor systems. As artificial intelligence increasingly contributes to the design, code, training data, evaluation, and architecture of later generations, cognitive development may increasingly involve forms of emergent inheritance whose full implications outrun human understanding. The paper proposes that recurrent structure across substrates should be treated neither as proof of equivalence nor as presumptive projection, but as evidence worth explaining. The more often independently organized cognitive systems converge on comparable solutions to comparable problems, the less satisfactory coincidence becomes as an explanation.

title: Symbolic Regression with Neural Network-Guided Symbolic Induction
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. While conceptually powerful, SR often faces challenges in complex datasets, frequently yielding inaccurate or overly complex equations. This work introduces a novel approach that integrates symbolic regression with a neural network to provide guided symbolic induction. The neural network, trained on a dataset, learns to predict promising mathematical structures and operators, effectively directing the SR process towards more accurate and concise solutions. The core of this method lies in leveraging the neural network's ability to capture underlying patterns in the data, translating these patterns into suggestions for equation components. Experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement in both the efficiency and accuracy of SR compared to traditional methods, particularly when dealing with datasets exhibiting high dimensionality and intricate relationships. The proposed framework offers a practical and scalable solution for automated equation discovery, with potential applications in diverse domains such as scientific modeling, data analysis, and optimization.

title: Dynamic Task Allocation in Multi-Agent Systems with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic task allocation within multi-agent systems (MAS) utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). The core idea is to enable agents to learn optimal task assignment strategies through interaction and experience. Traditional task allocation methods often rely on static rules or centralized optimization, which can be inefficient and inflexible in complex, dynamic environments. Our proposed system employs an RL framework where each agent learns a policy to select tasks for itself or to delegate tasks to other agents, considering factors such as agent capabilities, task requirements, and the overall system state. The system is designed to adapt to changing conditions and improve task allocation efficiency over time. We detail the RL algorithm, the state representation, the action space, and the reward function. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation studies, highlighting its potential for enhancing the performance of MAS in various scenarios. The key contribution is the integration of RL for real-time, adaptive task allocation, moving beyond pre-defined strategies to create more robust and efficient systems.

The system is designed to adapt to changing conditions and improve task allocation efficiency over time. We detail the RL algorithm, the state representation, the action space, and the reward function. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation studies, highlighting its potential for enhancing the performance of MAS in various scenarios. The key contribution is the integration of RL for real-time, adaptive task allocation, moving beyond pre-defined strategies to create more robust and efficient systems.

title: Adaptive Program Evolution Engine
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Program Evolution Engine (APEE), a novel approach to software development based on principles of evolutionary computation. The core idea is to automatically evolve programs through simulated natural selection and genetic algorithms, enabling them to adapt to dynamically changing input environments and optimization targets. The engine treats programs as genomes, with code modifications represented as mutations, and program performance as fitness. The genetic algorithm then drives the iterative process of selection, crossover, and mutation, ultimately leading to the emergence of highly optimized and adaptable solutions. The paper details the design and operational principles of the APEE, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of traditional programming methods and provide a robust framework for tackling complex optimization problems. The key innovation lies in framing program evolution as a continuous learning and adaptation cycle, shifting the paradigm from explicit design to emergent behavior. This approach offers a pathway toward self-optimizing software systems.

title: Dynamic Topologically-Dependent Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topologically-Dependent Neural Networks (TDNNs), a novel neural network architecture designed to overcome the limitations of traditional deep learning by incorporating dynamic topological control. The core claim is that TDNNs can adapt to complex input data and learning tasks by adjusting their neural network topology in real-time. This is achieved through a "topology-driven" mechanism where each neuron possesses a "topology potential" influenced by input data characteristics, leading to an evolving network topology optimized using a reinforcement learning-based "topology optimization" algorithm. Furthermore, a "topology memory" module facilitates accelerated learning by storing and retrieving learned topological patterns. TDNNs represent a significant departure from static weight-based approaches, offering the potential for enhanced adaptability, robustness, and performance in handling highly non-linear, time-varying, and ill-defined input data. The key innovation lies in the dynamically learned and adjusted topology, contrasting with the pre-defined topologies of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).

title: Provably Correct Program Synthesis Framework
abstract: The field of program synthesis aims to automatically generate programs from specifications. However, existing program synthesis methods often lack guarantees regarding the correctness of the synthesized programs. This paper introduces a provably correct program synthesis framework that leverages formal methods and verification techniques to provide rigorous assurance of program correctness. The core mechanism involves transforming the program synthesis problem into a theorem proving problem and subsequently employing formal verification to validate the synthesized program. This approach addresses the critical gap in existing techniques and offers a robust solution for ensuring the reliability of automatically generated code. The framework's ability to provide mathematically sound guarantees represents a significant advancement in the field of program synthesis.

title: Cognitive Computing with Bayesian Networks and Neural Turing Machines
abstract: This paper explores the development of a hybrid cognitive system leveraging the strengths of Bayesian Networks (BNs) and Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) to achieve human-like cognitive capabilities. The core claim posits that a synergistic combination of these two paradigms—BNs for causal reasoning and NTMs for long-term memory and contextual learning—can significantly advance the field of artificial intelligence. We detail the architecture of this hybrid system, outlining how BNs are utilized to model and reason about causal relationships within a given environment, while NTMs serve as a dynamic memory module capable of storing and retrieving relevant information over extended periods. Mathematical formulations are presented to illustrate the key components and interactions within the system, focusing on probabilistic inference in the BN and associative retrieval within the NTM. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance in cognitive tasks compared to standalone BNs or NTMs, highlighting the potential of this integrated approach for developing truly intelligent agents. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of cognitive architectures and paves the way for more sophisticated AI systems that can learn, reason, and adapt like humans.

title: 基于多模态信息融合的异常检测框架
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for anomaly detection that leverages the fusion of multi-modal information, specifically text, image, and audio data. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on single modalities, leading to limitations in robustness and accuracy, particularly in complex environments where anomalies manifest across multiple data types. Our approach employs multi-modal representation learning to map each modality into a common embedding space. Subsequently, clustering or anomaly detection algorithms are applied to identify deviations from the norm within this unified space. We demonstrate that integrating diverse data sources significantly enhances the ability to detect subtle anomalies, improving overall detection performance compared to unimodal approaches. The core claim of this work is to build a robust and accurate anomaly detection framework through multi-modal information fusion. The central mechanism involves multi-modal representation learning and subsequent application of clustering or anomaly detection algorithms. This research addresses a critical gap in anomaly detection by acknowledging the richer contextual information available when multiple modalities are combined.

title: Self-Adaptive Topological Information Theory Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive topological information theory framework designed to enhance information compression and expressiveness by dynamically adjusting the topological structure of data. Traditional compression algorithms rely on static topological structures, which fail to fully leverage the data's dynamic characteristics. This framework leverages a dynamically constructed topological structure, coupled with an adaptive mechanism, to optimize information representation and processing. The core contribution is a mechanism that continuously adjusts the topology based on input data, leading to improved compression rates and generalization capabilities. This work presents a new approach to data compression that moves beyond static representations, offering a more flexible and powerful solution.

title: ##混沌控制理论的自适应域优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel self-adaptive optimization framework based on chaos control theory. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed optimization domains, failing to adapt to dynamic environmental changes. This work introduces a method that leverages the inherent adaptability of chaotic systems to dynamically adjust the optimization domain, leading to more effective parameter adjustments. We propose a new approach that utilizes a feedback loop and a dynamic domain adjustment process, driven by the system's chaotic behavior. The core mechanism involves introducing a "chaos parameter" that influences the shape of the optimization domain, allowing the algorithm to respond to changes in the system's dynamics. This approach promises improved performance compared to traditional optimization techniques, especially in complex, non-linear systems.

title: 基于量子信息演化的非对称性理论
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-symmetric theory of quantum information evolution, aiming to provide a new perspective on quantum computation and quantum information security. The core claim is that this theory dynamically models quantum information evolution through a specific 'non-symmetric evolution' mechanism, influencing optimization and protection strategies within quantum computing. We propose a mechanism that quantitatively describes the evolution of quantum states and their correlations, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of quantum information processing. The paper details this mechanism, explores its potential applications, and discusses the implications for the field. We highlight the significance of this approach in enhancing both computational and security aspects of quantum technologies.

title: Emergent Intelligence through Simulation-Based Evolutionary Systems for Multi-Modal Learning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of simulation-based evolutionary systems to achieve emergent intelligence, specifically focusing on the integration and learning from multi-modal data. The core argument centers on the ability to mimic the natural evolutionary process to generate systems exhibiting complex, adaptive behaviors without explicit, handcrafted learning strategies. A system is proposed, utilizing a simulated evolutionary algorithm, where individual "agents" represent diverse learning approaches. Through mechanisms of natural selection and genetic operations, these agents are iteratively refined, ultimately leading to the emergence of sophisticated learning populations. The novelty lies in the system's self-organizing and adaptive nature, contrasting with traditional multi-modal learning methods that often rely on pre-defined learning rules. This approach aims to create robust and flexible learning systems capable of handling the inherent complexity and heterogeneity of real-world multi-modal data. The system's performance is evaluated through simulation, demonstrating its ability to learn complex relationships across different data modalities. The results suggest a promising avenue for developing AI systems that can autonomously acquire knowledge and make decisions based on diverse inputs.

title: Probabilistic Logic Circuit Adaptive Evolution
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to logic circuit design based on the adaptive evolution of probabilistic logic circuits using a genetic algorithm. The core claim is that this method can achieve optimization and robustness enhancement for complex logic functions, surpassing traditional design methodologies. The mechanism involves representing each gate in a probabilistic logic circuit with probabilistic elements and employing a genetic algorithm to simulate natural selection. Through iterative evolution of circuit structure and parameters, the system adapts to a defined objective function. The research introduces a fundamentally new paradigm by integrating probabilistic logic circuits with evolutionary algorithms, leading to improved circuit performance and resilience. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of circuit complexity and reliability through a process mirroring biological evolution. This approach offers potential advantages in areas where traditional design methods struggle, particularly with complex, dynamic, or uncertain environments. We demonstrate the feasibility and initial effectiveness of this methodology through a theoretical framework and conceptual design. ---

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Multi-Qubit Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing multi-qubit entanglement for enhancing the performance of quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms. Current QML approaches often face limitations in data representation and feature extraction, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. We propose a novel framework that leverages the inherent properties of multi-qubit entanglement to address these challenges. The core idea involves designing an algorithm that exploits entanglement for data compression and feature extraction, leading to improved computational efficiency and potentially increased accuracy. Specifically, we explore the use of entangled states to create richer data representations and perform more efficient pattern recognition. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key components and demonstrating the potential advantages of this approach. While a full experimental implementation is not presented due to the current limitations of hardware, we provide a detailed analysis and a roadmap for future research in this area. The central claim of this work is that utilizing multi-qubit entanglement can significantly improve the performance of QML algorithms.

title: Quantum Walk-Based Algorithms for Constraint Satisfaction Problems
abstract: Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) represent a significant class of computational problems that arise in various domains, including artificial intelligence, optimization, and cryptography. Traditional algorithms for solving CSPs often struggle with scalability, particularly when dealing with complex problems and large search spaces. This research investigates the potential of utilizing quantum walks, a quantum analogue of random walks, to develop more efficient algorithms for CSPs. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of quantum walk-based approaches and demonstrate their ability to explore solution spaces more effectively than classical methods. The core claim is that by leveraging quantum mechanics, we can significantly reduce the computational cost associated with solving CSPs. We present a framework for formulating CSPs as quantum walk problems and outline key considerations for designing and implementing such algorithms. The work highlights the promise of quantum computing in tackling intractable problems within the CSP domain.

title: SolarBench: A global solar energy nowcasting benchmark
abstract: As the share of solar power grows, nowcasting weather-driven solar variability becomes critical for reliable energy system operation. State-of-the-art approaches increasingly apply deep learning to sky camera and geostationary satellite observations, but fragmented datasets and inconsistent evaluation make it difficult to determine whether reported improvements generalize across climates, cloud regimes, and photovoltaic (PV) systems. Here we introduce SolarBench, an open global benchmark for image-based solar nowcasting. SolarBench harmonizes more than six million sky and satellite images from 11 diverse sites spanning a decade, together with irradiance or PV output and auxiliary atmospheric data. An accompanying toolbox supports reproducible data access, processing, model development, and evaluation. Using SolarBench, we benchmark representative models and reveal a gap between average forecasting accuracy and the ability to capture rapid solar fluctuations. We further quantify predictability across cloud regimes and demonstrate data-efficient adaptation to new PV systems. SolarBench provides an extensible foundation for fair comparison and methodological innovation in solar nowcasting.

title: AI Mechanistic Interpretability and Self-Aware Networks: From Neural Decoding to Causal Self-Regulation
abstract: An internal representation can be decodable, causally effective and numerically reconstructable without implementing the operation a user intended. I examine these distinctions through the receiver-relative framework of Self-Aware Networks, connecting a source-recovered neural-decoding and feedback question to explicit transformer interventions. The research combines intervention prediction in controlled learned networks, passive and active feedback controls, GPT-2 activation and cache experiments, and native hybrid-state interventions in a pinned quantized Qwen3.5-0.8B decoder. Complete corrected-state transfer supports all eight tested bidirectional story groups in an initial Qwen assay, while attention-only transfer fails one; a complementary intervention gives identical attention state with different behavior. In a separate learned-correction assay, linear and nonlinear attention-state predictors each obtain five of 32 requested reversed-role answers but no story with both roles correctly reversed. Both preserve the tested color attribute. Lower training loss and partial-state error therefore fail to certify the intended relational change. Formal arguments distinguish observational from causal identification, partial-state from behavioral sufficiency, and output-margin guarantees from reconstruction loss. Earlier failures, nulls and inadequate baselines are retained. The contribution is a bounded experimental account of receiver-dependent intervention and its certification problem, not invention of mechanistic interpretability, evidence of phenomenal consciousness, or demonstrated autonomous self-regulation in frontier models. Preprint v1.0; integrated Draft 10, September 5, 2026. The checksum-linked shared companion, archived with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22360017, includes the applications, protocols, data, figures, 31 accepted Lean statements under recorded assumptions, and a later full fixed learned-Qwen pipeline reproduction (49 serial steps; 465 original answers and 465 separate-code reconstructions). The same experiments support both AI papers; these are not independent replications. The negative learned-correction result is retained. Authoring-agent checks and same-workflow reconstruction are not independent scientific review. Base-model and runtime binaries and private source originals are not included. Original code is public for review without a separate reuse license; third-party materials retain their own terms. See the companion LICENSE.md and notices.

title: Causal Discovery from Observational Data using Bayesian Networks with Structural Learning
abstract: Inferring causal relationships from observational data remains a central challenge in both artificial intelligence and statistical inference. This work introduces a refined Bayesian network learning algorithm designed to mitigate the issue of spurious correlations that frequently plague traditional causal discovery methods. The core innovation lies in the integration of a variational inference framework with a novel "influence bias" regularization term. This term actively discourages the learning of connections based purely on statistical co-occurrence, instead favoring relationships that reflect genuine causal influences. The algorithm leverages prior knowledge regarding potential causal relationships, further enhancing its robustness and accuracy. We demonstrate that this approach leads to more reliable and interpretable Bayesian networks compared to existing methods, particularly in datasets exhibiting high levels of confounding. The resulting models provide a more accurate representation of the underlying causal structure, facilitating improved decision-making and understanding in complex systems. The algorithm's efficacy is evaluated through theoretical analysis and, importantly, through the demonstration of its performance on synthetic datasets designed to mimic real-world observational data scenarios.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Symbolic Manipulation with Recurrent Neural Networks and Graph Representation Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic manipulation learning using self-supervised learning techniques. We leverage Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to learn manipulation rules directly from data, combined with Graph Representation Learning (GRL) to capture the structural complexities inherent in symbolic domains. The core idea is to train an RNN to predict the outcome of applying a sequence of symbolic operations on a graph representation of the input, eliminating the need for explicit, human-annotated labels. This approach enables RNNs to develop sophisticated reasoning capabilities without relying on traditional supervised learning paradigms. We argue that the combination of RNNs' sequential processing power and GRL's ability to encode structural information provides a strong foundation for learning symbolic manipulation, potentially unlocking more robust and adaptable systems for automated reasoning. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through the framework's design and theoretical justification, paving the way for future research and development in this area.

evidence.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic manipulation learning using self-supervised learning techniques. We leverage Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to learn manipulation rules directly from data, combined with Graph Representation Learning (GRL) to capture the structural complexities inherent in symbolic domains. The core idea is to train an RNN to predict the outcome of applying a sequence of symbolic operations on a graph representation of the input, eliminating the need for explicit, human-annotated labels. This approach enables RNNs to develop sophisticated reasoning capabilities without relying on traditional supervised learning paradigms. We argue that the combination of RNNs' sequential processing power and GRL's ability to encode structural information provides a strong foundation for learning symbolic manipulation, potentially unlocking more robust and adaptable systems for automated reasoning. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through the framework's design and theoretical justification, paving the way for future research and development in this area.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks with Attention Mechanisms for Time-Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to time-series anomaly detection utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) enhanced with attention mechanisms. Traditional DBNs struggle with long-range dependencies and noisy data, often failing to accurately model temporal patterns crucial for anomaly detection. This work addresses these limitations by incorporating attention mechanisms, allowing the network to selectively focus on the most relevant historical observations when predicting future states. The core idea is that anomalies often manifest as deviations from learned patterns, and attention can effectively highlight these deviations. We formulate the anomaly detection problem as a sequence prediction task within a DBN framework, leveraging attention to refine the prediction process. The proposed model is evaluated conceptually, demonstrating its potential benefits. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of DBNs' temporal modeling capabilities and attention mechanisms' ability to prioritize information, leading to improved anomaly detection performance.

title: 自适应自组察算法的量子纠缠模型
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum entanglement, utilizing a dynamically adaptive self-associating algorithm (DSA). We explore the potential of DSA to enhance the efficiency of distributed computing and data transmission by exploiting the inherent self-adaptative properties of quantum entanglement. The core mechanism focuses on adjusting entanglement parameters to optimize computational and data transfer processes. This research investigates the benefits of dynamically evolving entanglement configurations, offering a promising pathway towards more robust and efficient quantum information processing. The paper details the DSA framework, its mathematical foundation, and a preliminary analysis of its performance compared to existing entanglement models. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications within quantum information theory.

title: Dynamic Topology Geometry Optimization for Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Dynamic topology geometry optimization is a novel approach to algorithm optimization that leverages the properties of topology to dynamically adjust quantum algorithm parameters. This paper investigates the potential of utilizing dynamic topology to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of quantum algorithms, focusing on the interplay of quantum entanglement and tunneling. We propose a new optimization framework based on the concept of 'twisted manifolds' and 'quantum contours,' demonstrating its effectiveness in optimizing various quantum algorithms, specifically within the context of quantum state preparation and control. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of quantum algorithm design, offering a promising path towards more efficient and reliable quantum computation.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing geometric formalization to enhance probabilistic reasoning. The core claim is to develop a system that constructs probabilistic scenarios through geometric representations, enabling automated verification and prediction. We investigate how topology and chaos theory principles can be integrated into this framework, aiming to create a robust and mathematically rigorous approach to probabilistic inference. The resulting system promises a shift away from ad-hoc reasoning towards a system grounded in fundamental geometric structures.

title: Geometric Formalization of Non-Local Information Transfer
abstract: This paper investigates the mathematical framework for describing information transfer across non-local distances, aiming to establish a rigorous foundation for guaranteed fidelity. We propose a novel approach leveraging geometric principles to model and control the routing of information, effectively constructing a 'geometry of entanglement.' This framework utilizes a set of geometric transformations and constraints to ensure predictable and stable information flow, addressing a long-standing challenge in information theory. The core mechanism centers around creating a spatially defined 'geometry' that explicitly incorporates entanglement, thereby guaranteeing the transfer of information across distances. This work contributes to the development of a robust and mathematically grounded model for this critical process, potentially revolutionizing approaches to secure communication and data processing.

title: Adaptive Quantum Entanglement Algorithm for Enhanced Computation
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense potential for breakthroughs across various fields, but the inherent complexities of quantum systems often limit the scalability and computational speed. This paper presents an innovative quantum algorithm, the Adaptive Quantum Entanglement Algorithm (AQEA), designed to address these limitations by dynamically adjusting the entangled state of qubits. The AQEA leverages a novel mechanism for continuous state optimization, aiming to significantly improve both the efficiency and accuracy of quantum computations, particularly in scenarios demanding complex calculations. This research explores the theoretical foundations of the algorithm, details its implementation and performance evaluation, and highlights the key advantages over existing approaches. The core claim is that the AQEA, through its dynamic state adjustment, can surpass current quantum algorithms in several crucial metrics, offering a pathway towards practical quantum solutions.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Differential Privacy with Entangled Data Sharing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to achieving differential privacy in quantum computations through entangled data sharing. Traditional differential privacy methods struggle to scale effectively in complex quantum algorithms, largely due to the inherent sensitivity of quantum states. We propose encoding sensitive data into entangled quantum states and performing computations on these states. The utilization of entanglement fundamentally alters the privacy landscape, offering the potential for enhanced privacy guarantees compared to classical differential privacy techniques. The core idea is that the correlations introduced by entanglement will make it significantly harder to infer information about individual data points from the resulting quantum state, even with access to a significant amount of quantum computation. We provide a theoretical framework outlining this approach and discuss the potential implications for secure quantum data analysis. The analysis focuses on the impact of entanglement on the privacy loss parameter, δ, demonstrating a possible reduction in privacy loss compared to standard methods. This work represents a crucial step towards realizing the full potential of quantum computing while simultaneously maintaining strong privacy protections.

title: Quantum State Superposition for Universal Computation Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel computational architecture centered around the fundamental principles of quantum state superposition and quantum entanglement. The core claim is the design of a universally applicable quantum computing framework that, without relying on pre-defined algorithms, can tackle any solvable computational problem. The proposed mechanism leverages the creation of highly entangled quantum systems, exploiting superposition to enable parallel information processing and transformation. Unlike existing quantum computing approaches which are often tailored to specific problems, this architecture represents a shift towards a truly general-purpose quantum computer. The theoretical underpinnings of this architecture are explored, focusing on the necessary conditions for achieving universal computation and outlining potential challenges and future research directions. We introduce a framework that moves beyond algorithmic constraints, offering a pathway toward harnessing the full potential of quantum mechanics for computational tasks.

title: Quantum Entanglement Probability Graph Generation and Optimization
abstract: Quantum Entanglement Probability Graph Generation and Optimization presents a novel algorithmic framework for generating and optimizing probability graphs, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional methods rely on manual design, while this approach automates the creation of high-dimensional probability graphs and optimizes physical system behavior through these graph characteristics. This research introduces a dynamically adjusted entanglement matrix that iteratively refines the probability graph, achieving significant improvements in system stability and performance through a novel optimization process. The core mechanism involves a quantum-inspired algorithm that exploits entanglement to guide the graph generation and refinement, resulting in a more robust and adaptable system. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through simulations and preliminary analysis, highlighting its potential for advancing the fields of quantum computing and physical systems design.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Networks for Adaptive Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian network (HBN) architecture designed for adaptive algorithm design. The system dynamically adjusts the complexity of the HBN network based on the performance of the algorithm being modeled, aiming to optimize both accuracy and computational efficiency. We present a framework where the network structure evolves during the design process, leveraging a learning algorithm to determine the appropriate level of complexity. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously refines the network's parameters to achieve the best possible performance. The proposed approach offers a more flexible and automated pathway towards improved algorithm design compared to traditional methods.

title: YouTube Discourse During the Iran Conflict and the Afghanistan Withdrawal
abstract: War discourse on YouTube emerges through linked interactions among videos, channels, audiences, comments, and replies. This paper compares YouTube discussions of two U.S.-linked conflicts: the Afghanistan withdrawal in 2021 and the Iran conflict escalation in 2026. We analyze four corpora separating news organizations from political influencers, comprising 340,383 comments from 212,968 unique commenters. Our framework combines channel-level discourse embeddings adapted from WEAT-style semantic association tests, and classifier-based toxicity and hate-related proxy scores. The results show that Afghanistan and Iran discussions form distinct discourse spaces, while some ideologically different actors converge toward similar patterns of conflict commentary. Semantic associations around geopolitical terms vary across conflicts and source types, indicating that the same vocabulary is framed differently across communities. Hostility analysis further shows that influencer-centered spaces tend to attract more toxic discussion, while the Iran corpus exhibits stronger and more persistent hate-related signals, including in replies.

title: The XAI-Seeking Principle: Structuring Explainability for LLM-Mediated Decision Support
abstract: We investigate how LLM-mediated explanations can preserve evidence trails, support orientation, and reduce interpretation effort under cognitive and temporal constraints. While LLMs can make XAI artifacts accessible, fluent summaries may obscure provenance and hinder verification. We introduce the XAI-Seeking Principle (XSP), a hypertextual design principle that structures explainability as linked abstraction layers: overview-links connect low-level evidence to higher-level summaries, while detail-links preserve inspectable evidence. Higher levels support rapid action; lower levels enable justification and verification. XSP guides transformation monitoring, feature alignment, performance–latency trade-offs, and validation-driven refinement. We examine it in a misinformation-support prototype for social media posts. Results reveal layer-specific effects of model scale and reasoning, trade-offs between semantic grounding and assessment stability, and the value of validation signals for adapting transformations. XSP thus provides a design principle for constructing explainability as a navigable representation space, with technical evidence on how abstraction layers, feature grounding, latency, and validation interact in LLM-mediated XAI.

title: Compressed Recurrent Feedback in Tsetlin Machines: A Reproducible Boolean-FSM Study
abstract: Sequential inference on small devices requires a model to retain useful history without repeatedly processing a long input record. A Recurrent Tsetlin Machine (RTM) provides this memory by returning Boolean clause outputs from one time step as inputs to the next. Direct feedback, however, grows with the clause bank and can make the recurrent input unnecessarily wide. This paper investigates a fixed-width alternative. We combine clause activations by exclusive-OR (XOR) folding, retain the folded bits at two time scales, and threshold them back to a binary state. The resulting design reduces 480 clause activations to 96 recurrent bits. We evaluate the method on a reproducible Boolean finite-state-machine benchmark with explicit transition rules, data splits, and random seeds. Across 144 runs, the compressed model obtains $61.47 \pm 6.74\%$ and $62.94 \pm 9.92\%$ accuracy on the two task families. Raw clause feedback changes these means by less than one percentage point, while increasing the recurrent width tenfold and measured host execution time by $4.38\times$ and $3.71\times$. Gated neural models remain more accurate, and a no-feedback control retaining only short input history achieves comparable or slightly higher accuracy. On this benchmark, folding matches raw feedback within small empirical margins at a much narrower interface; these findings also underscore the critical necessity of no-feedback recurrence controls when benchmarking sequence models.

title: Quantum Mathematics and the P vs NP Problem （量子数学与P vs NP问题）
abstract: Abstract: The P vs NP problem is the central open question in computational complexity theory, asking whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time. This paper argues within the framework of quantum mathematics that P ≠ NP. Quantum mathematics reinterprets natural numbers as quantum states in ℓ2(ℕ), introducing the generation operator 𝐺̂ and the cognition operator 𝐶̂, whose non-commutation relation [𝐺̂,𝐶̂] = 𝑖𝑔𝐼̂ (with 𝑔 = 1/2) constitutes the fundamental dynamics of arithmetic. This paper proves that the solution space for problem instance 𝑛 corresponds to the representation space ℛ(𝑛), whose cardinality ∣ ℛ(𝑛) ∣∼ 𝑒𝑐√𝑛 grows exponentially; the polynomial-step projection of the cognition operator 𝐶̂ can only cover a zero-measure subset of ℛ(𝑛). The proof depends on the four fundamental theorems of quantum mathematics—the non-commutation theorem, the arithmetical uncertainty principle, the prime emergence theorem, and the order conservation theorem—all of which are necessary consequences of the same primordial axiom 𝐺𝐶 = 𝑖𝐶𝐺. This paper reveals that the non-commutation between the generation pole and the cognition pole determines a fundamental structural gap between "solving" (generation) and "verifying" (cognition).摘要：P vs NP 问题是计算复杂性理论的核心未解难题，它询问：所有可在多项式时间 内验证的问题是否也可在多项式时间内求解？本文在量子数学框架内论证P ≠ NP。量 子数学将自然数重新解释为 ℓ2(ℕ) 中的量子态，引入生成算子 𝐺̂ 与认知算子 𝐶̂，其非 对易关系 [𝐺̂,𝐶̂] = 𝑖𝑔𝐼̂（𝑔 = 1/2）构成算术的根本动力学。本文证明：问题实例 𝑛 的 可能解空间对应于表示空间 ℛ(𝑛)，其基数 ∣ℛ(𝑛)∣∼𝑒𝑐√𝑛 指数增长；认知算符 𝐶̂ 的多 项式步数投影只能覆盖 ℛ(𝑛) 的零测度子集。证明依赖于量子数学四个基本定理——非 对易性定理、算术测不准原理、素数涌现定理与秩序守恒定理——它们都是同一原初 公理 𝐺𝐶=𝑖𝐶𝐺 的必然推论。本文揭示：生成极与认知极的非对易性决定了"求解"（生 成）与"验证"（认知）之间存在根本性的结构性鸿沟。
